newsitem.title: THAILAND: Big spending spree seen ahead of Thai election.
newsitem.headline: Big spending spree seen ahead of Thai election.

text.p: An estimated 20 billion baht ($800 million) will be spent by politicians in the run up to Thailand's general election set for November 17, a research centre said on Tuesday.
The Thai Farmers Research Center Co Ltd said in a study obtained by Reuters that the amount spent would be 20 percent higher than that spent in the July 1995 election campaign.

The nation's second snap election in just over 16 months was called in late September when outgoing Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa dissolved parliament following a fall-out with his coalition partners.
The Thai Farmers survey said that the 2,310 candidates from 13 political parties vying for 393 seats in parliament would spend an average 8.7 million baht each.

Much of that money -- about 3.53 billion baht, or 18 percent -- would be spent in the country's impoverished northeast where the majority of parliamentary seats are located and the contest is expected to be intense, it added.

"The study has found out that competition in the northeast is the most cut-throat scene compared to other regions," it added. Over 1,000 candidates are standing for the 137 seats at stake in the region.
Academics and political analysts agreed with the findings of the Thai Farmers survey and said much of the money would be spent on vote-buying, rallies and other campaign needs.

"Vote-buying has become a common phenomenon in Thai elections. This practice will intensify because there is a clear polarisation of political parties," said Chaiwat Khamchoo, a political scientist at Chulalongkorn University.

Only two parties -- the New Aspiration Party (NAP) led by outgoing defence minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh and the Democrat Party of former premier Chuan Leekpai -- were seen as top contenders to lead the next coalition government, he said.
In the past there were three or four parties with an equal chance to win the most seats. "So in the last minute money could become the decisive factor in this polls," Chaiwat said.

Thai Farmers said 45.6 percent of the 3,713 respondents felt vote-buying was more rampant in the current election campaign than in the last one, 10.5 percent said it was reduced and 43.9 percent said the situation was largely unchanged.
"The good news is that Thais are against vote-buying," it said, adding that, "89.6 percent of (the) voters do not agree with vote-buying at all."

When asked if they would take goods or money offered by politicians, 60.2 percent said they would. But 95 percent said they would not vote for politicians they did not like, even if they were offered gifts.
The group said money spent by political parties on the election would benefit not only voters and but various businesses throughout the country as well.
